surprise.title: 55 years ago today, Intel released the 4004, the chip that started the CPU story you study for A+
surprise.body: On November 15, 1971, Intel released the 4004, the first in its long line of central processing units. It was a 4-bit chip with just 2,300 transistors, a clock speed of about 740 kHz, and a 16-pin package, built on a 10-micrometer process, and it sold for $60. It was designed for a Busicom calculator, yet it became the first significant commercial example of putting a whole processor on one chip. Exactly thirty years later, on November 15, 2001, Microsoft launched the original Xbox in North America, and its Intel Pentium III ran at 733 MHz, roughly a thousand times faster, which means today the Xbox turns 25 as well. Every time a Core 1 question asks about clock speed, cores, or sockets, you are looking at the great-grandchildren of that little calculator chip. It is a clear, crisp Sunday in Tallahassee, about 36°F early with a high near 60°F, clouds rolling in after 2 PM, sunset at 5:40 PM, and 28 days until you sail out of Tampa.
